title: Hexagon x Redwood — Dedicated autoscaling bounds (discovery)
topics: Dedicated capacity overview and current scaling behavior
Hard min/max bounds to control spend and ensure baseline SLO
Predictable daily ramps vs unpredictable burst traffic
Predictive scaling ideas (time-of-day, scheduled events) and safety rails
Pilot + rollout timeline and enablement path
summary: Hexagon described recurring budget surprises due to reactive scale-ups on Dedicated plus periodic burst traffic tied to incident-response workflows and customer batch jobs. They want contractual-like guardrails: a hard maximum to cap spend, plus a minimum baseline to protect p95 latency during known ramps. Redwood discussed upcoming autoscaling bounds semantics (min/max hard clamp, cooldowns, deterministic decision reasons) and an optional predictive mode that biases scale-up ahead of traffic ramps while still allowing reactive signals to override when predictions are wrong (but never violating bounds). Next steps include Hexagon sharing traffic patterns and budget targets, Redwood sharing draft semantics + pilot timing, and scheduling a technical deep dive on signals and observability.
next_steps: Hexagon to send 2–3 weeks of request rate + token throughput traces (or summarized hourly patterns) and current SLO targets.
Redwood to share draft semantics for min/max bounds and how they interact with platform defaults + overload behavior.
Schedule technical deep dive focused on predictive scaling inputs, staleness behavior, and dashboards/alerts (Roberto + Evan with Vanessa).
Follow-up in 1 week to confirm pilot eligibility and preferred region(s).
action_items: Owner: Liam O'Rourke — Send recap email with pilot timeline, feature-flag enablement process, and list of required data from Hexagon — Due: 2025-05-15
Owner: Lauren Bishop — Share PRD-level semantics excerpt (hard max cap, min baseline, precedence, and 'what happens when max is hit') — Due: 2025-05-17
Owner: Vanessa Ortiz — Provide a short technical note on autoscaler signals (queue depth vs saturation) and proposed predictive interface/fallback — Due: 2025-05-20
Owner: Maya Chen — Confirm target monthly spend ceiling and acceptable short-term overshoot (if any) plus internal approvals for pilot — Due: 2025-05-21
Owner: Roberto Alvarez — Share existing alert thresholds and examples of incidents where scaling was too late or too expensive — Due: 2025-05-21
transcript:
Meeting: Hexagon x Redwood — Dedicated autoscaling bounds (discovery)
Recorded: 2025-05-14 4:00 PM PT
Duration: 52 minutes

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Liam O'Rourke (TAM), Lauren Bishop (Product, Dedicated), Vanessa Ortiz (Fleet Autoscaling)
Hexagon Support Systems: Maya Chen (Director, Platform Engineering), Roberto Alvarez (SRE Lead), Anika Patel (FinOps), Evan Brooks (Staff Backend)

---
Fireflies - Auto Summary (generated)
- Customer is seeing spend spikes from reactive autoscaling and wants hard max bounds.
- Customer also wants a minimum baseline to avoid queue buildup during predictable traffic ramps.
- Redwood is building per-deployment min/max scaling bounds + optional predictive scaling signals with guardrails.
- Discussed audit logs and RBAC for policy changes.

Questions captured
- If max bound is hit, how is that surfaced and what does Redwood do (alerts, routing, degraded mode)?
- Can Hexagon set different bounds by time of day?
- How do predictions work if traffic patterns shift (holidays, incidents)?
- Can config changes be managed via API/IaC and audited?

---

[00:00] Liam O'Rourke: Alright, I think we’re at time. Thanks everyone for joining. I’m Liam, I work with our Dedicated accounts. Lauren’s our PM for Dedicated, and Vanessa leads a bunch of the autoscaling work on the fleet side.

[00:14] Maya Chen: Hey. Maya here. I run platform engineering. Roberto is our SRE lead. Anika from FinOps. Evan is one of our backend folks who owns the LLM integration.

[00:24] Liam O'Rourke: Great. The agenda I sent was pretty lightweight—just understand what you’re trying to solve around scaling, bounds, budget, and then talk through what we have today versus what’s on the roadmap.

[00:35] Maya Chen: Sounds good.

[00:38] Liam O'Rourke: Maybe, Maya, you want to start with what’s prompting this? We saw the note about budget cap.

[00:44] Maya Chen: Yeah. So, we’re on Dedicated with you all in us-west. We love the latency when it’s stable, but the cost is… not stable. We have reactive scaling, which is fine in principle, but when we get certain bursts it scales up faster than our finance people expect.

[01:02] Anika Patel: Um, yeah. Like, it’s not like a 10% swing. It’s sometimes like, “Why did we just double the GPUs for two hours?” and then we get an invoice preview and it’s a fight.

[01:16] Evan Brooks: The bursts are kind of two types. One is predictable—like daily ramp when our support agents come online and customers do morning batch stuff. The other is unpredictable, like incident response. If a customer has an outage they’ll hammer the assistant feature and our traffic goes weird.

[01:34] Roberto Alvarez: And right now we can sort of manually clamp it by paging someone to go change a setting, but that defeats the point. It’s 2025. We can’t have a human be the governor.

[01:45] Liam O'Rourke: Yeah, makes sense. Just to calibrate, today are you using our default autoscaling policy? Like CPU/GPU saturation and queue depth-based triggers?

[01:55] Roberto Alvarez: I think it’s primarily queue depth plus some utilization. The problem is queue depth can spike and then it scales, but by the time it scales, we’re already late. And then it overshoots.

[02:06] Vanessa Ortiz: Yep. That’s consistent with what we see on some workloads: queue depth is a good “you’re in trouble” signal, but it’s not necessarily a good “avoid trouble” signal.

[02:16] Lauren Bishop: And just to connect this to the feature you asked about—what you’re describing is basically the two asks we’ve been hearing: one, “give me a hard ceiling so I can’t blow through spend,” and two, “help me not get caught flat-footed during ramps.”

[02:31] Maya Chen: Exactly. Hard ceiling, and also a baseline. Like we cannot go below some number because p95 blows up.

[02:39] Anika Patel: Baseline is actually easier to budget. The surprise is the scale-up beyond what we thought was possible.

[02:46] Liam O'Rourke: Got it. Can you share roughly your current replica range? Like number of GPUs or instances.

[02:53] Evan Brooks: I might get the number slightly wrong. I think we’re usually at like 8 A100 equivalents? And then it can jump to 16. Sometimes 20-ish? Not sure. We’re not always on the same SKU; there’s like mixed stuff sometimes.

[03:08] Vanessa Ortiz: For Dedicated it should be consistent within your pool, but there can be different instance sizes depending on how it was provisioned. We can look at the exact details later. The key part is you want “min” and “max” semantics in the policy.

[03:21] Maya Chen: Yes. But we want it hard. Not “best effort.” Like if we say max 16, it should never go to 18.

[03:28] Lauren Bishop: Understood. That’s actually the core requirement: max is an invariant. The autoscaler can recommend or request more, but the bounded desired gets clamped to your max.

[03:40] Roberto Alvarez: When you say “bounded desired,” does that mean we can see both numbers?

[03:44] Lauren Bishop: That’s the plan. Like requested desired vs bounded desired, and the reason code for why it changed. This is partly for debugging and partly for auditability.

[03:56] Anika Patel: That’s important. Because when finance asks “why did it scale,” I need an answer besides “the computer said so.”

[04:05] Liam O'Rourke: Totally. We’ve had other customers ask the same.

[04:09] Maya Chen: What happens though if we hit the max and traffic keeps going up? Do we just… drop requests?

[04:16] Vanessa Ortiz: Good question. The autoscaler can’t exceed the max, by definition. So the system will be in a bounded state. What happens end-to-end depends on your application config: you’ll see queueing increase, latency increase. We can also integrate that “bounded” signal upstream so routing can shed load or fall back if you have a fallback model.

[04:36] Evan Brooks: We do have a fallback to a smaller model in some cases, but we don’t want it to silently degrade.

[04:42] Lauren Bishop: Right, so the product direction is: we surface the “max-bound saturation” as a first-class condition. Console shows it, we emit metrics, and we can alert on it. Then you decide your policy: either accept the queueing, or configure fallback behavior. But the key is it’s explicit, not silent.

[05:01] Roberto Alvarez: So there would be an alert like “deployment is at max bound for X minutes and queue depth is rising.”

[05:08] Vanessa Ortiz: Exactly.

[05:10] Liam O'Rourke: Before we go too deep, can I ask—what’s the business constraint on max? Is it monthly spend, or is it like “we only bought N GPUs reserved”?

[05:20] Anika Patel: We have internal chargeback. We basically can’t exceed a monthly cap without VP approval. We can do it, but it’s painful. So we’d like to set max so we can’t exceed that cap by accident.

[05:34] Maya Chen: And we’d rather over-provision baseline than risk surprise. But only to a point.

[05:40] Evan Brooks: There’s also procurement timelines. If we decide we need more, it’s a planned change. It can’t be “oh it scaled to 40 GPUs because a customer clicked refresh.”

[05:51] Liam O'Rourke: Understood. And on the min side, what’s your “never go below” today? Is that like 8, as you said.

[06:00] Roberto Alvarez: Roughly. When it goes below that overnight, the morning ramp is brutal. Cold caches, cold… I’m going to say “KV cache” and I might be using the wrong term.

[06:10] Vanessa Ortiz: No, KV cache is right. There’s also general warm state, model weights are already loaded, batching dynamics. If you downscale too aggressively, you basically pay the warmup tax again.

[06:22] Roberto Alvarez: Exactly. So min helps avoid that.

[06:26] Lauren Bishop: The semantics we’re drafting are: min is also an invariant—autoscaler can’t go below it. There are some edge cases we’ll talk about, like if the region physically can’t satisfy min due to capacity shortage, but from a policy standpoint min is hard.

[06:43] Maya Chen: Wait, so region shortage could break min? That scares me.

[06:47] Vanessa Ortiz: It’s rare, but we want to be honest. If the GPUs aren’t available in the region, we can’t conjure them. In those cases, we surface a degraded state and page internally, and also notify you. But the autoscaler will keep trying and we won’t scale down further.

[07:05] Lauren Bishop: The product behavior is “min is intended as hard,” but reality sometimes means “unmet min” with clear visibility.

[07:12] Maya Chen: Ok. As long as it’s visible and not silent.

[07:16] Liam O'Rourke: That’s a good segue to observability and audit logs. Roberto, you mentioned you need reasons. Do you also need audit trails for config changes?

[07:25] Roberto Alvarez: Yeah. We’re SOC 2. Also internal change management. If someone changes min/max, we need to know who did it, when, and what it was before.

[07:36] Lauren Bishop: Yep. That’s in scope. Policy updates get logged as audit events with the actor (user or API token), timestamp, and the diff. And scaling decisions can also emit an audit-ish event with the reason codes.

[07:52] Evan Brooks: Can it be API driven? We use Terraform for most infra.

[07:56] Liam O'Rourke: Terraform support is on the list. In the initial pilot, it’s likely Console/API first, and then IaC shortly after. But the API semantics are the same.

[08:08] Anika Patel: For FinOps, we mostly need the max. But I want to understand—if we cap max, won’t we just see more timeouts and customer dissatisfaction?

[08:20] Maya Chen: That’s why we also want predictive. If we can scale ahead of the ramp, we don’t have to blow up at the spike.

[08:28] Lauren Bishop: Exactly. Predictive is optional. The way we’re thinking about it: you can enable predictive mode, and it provides a “suggested desired” based on forecast. But reactive signals like saturation and queue depth still override when forecast is wrong.

[08:45] Roberto Alvarez: Override meaning it will scale more than forecast says?

[08:48] Vanessa Ortiz: Yeah, it can scale up beyond the forecast suggestion if reactive says you’re in trouble. But it still can’t exceed max. And it still can’t go below min.

[09:00] Evan Brooks: So prediction is like a bias or head start.

[09:03] Vanessa Ortiz: Exactly. It’s not an autopilot that ignores reality.

[09:08] Maya Chen: What’s the forecast based on? Like, do we have to send you a schedule?

[09:14] Lauren Bishop: There are a couple modes we’re exploring. One is time-of-day patterns learned from history. Another is explicit scheduled events—like “every weekday 8am local, expect +X.” We’re starting with the simplest and safest: historical patterns plus a staleness check.

[09:33] Roberto Alvarez: Staleness check like if it hasn’t updated in a while, it won’t use it.

[09:37] Vanessa Ortiz: Exactly. If prediction data is stale or missing, the system falls back to reactive scaling. And we also clamp down to avoid weird outcomes like predicting null and scaling to zero—just as an example.

[09:52] Evan Brooks: Yeah, please don’t scale to zero.

[09:55] Lauren Bishop: (laughs) Yeah. The default for Dedicated is never scale to zero; and min bound makes it explicit.

[10:04] Liam O'Rourke: Can you talk us through your ramp pattern? Is it like a sharp step function at 9am or more gradual.

[10:12] Evan Brooks: It’s pretty repeatable. 7:30 to 9:30 local time we climb. But we also have a lunch bump, and then end-of-day in Europe, since we have some EU customers too.

[10:26] Maya Chen: We also do batch summarizations at night. Those are scheduled jobs. But the unpredictable one is incidents.

[10:35] Roberto Alvarez: Incidents are where queue depth goes 0 to 100 really fast.

[10:40] Vanessa Ortiz: For incidents, predictive is hard unless you can give us a leading signal. But the reactive component should catch it. The bounds are the tradeoff: do you want to allow the autoscaler to go high to protect SLO during incidents, or do you prefer hard cost ceiling even if you degrade.

[10:59] Anika Patel: Hard ceiling. We can degrade. But we need to know and we need a plan.

[11:05] Maya Chen: I’ll qualify that: Hard ceiling unless there’s an explicit exception. Like maybe we do a temporary change with approval.

[11:12] Liam O'Rourke: That’s a common pattern: keep max conservative, and then have a documented playbook to temporarily raise max for planned events.

[11:20] Roberto Alvarez: But then you need rate limiting on changes too. Because if someone scripts it wrong—

[11:25] Vanessa Ortiz: Yeah, we’re also adding guardrails around config churn. Like you can’t flip min/max every minute.

[11:33] Evan Brooks: That would be great.

[11:36] Liam O'Rourke: Switching gears for a second—are you evaluating other platforms? Just so we understand the bar.

[11:42] Maya Chen: We looked at Bedrock a bit, but we don’t love the performance predictability. OpenAI we used early, but data control and cost were rough. Together is on a shortlist.

[11:54] Evan Brooks: We also looked at SageMaker endpoints, but we don’t want to run all the operational stuff.

[12:00] Lauren Bishop: That makes sense. Dedicated is meant to give you that predictable operational layer without you owning the full autoscaler logic.

[12:08] Roberto Alvarez: Except we kinda want to own a piece of it—like the bounds.

[12:11] Lauren Bishop: Totally. Think of it as: you declare guardrails, we run the engine.

[12:18] Liam O'Rourke: Let’s talk about what you’d want to see in product. Console settings? API? Both?

[12:26] Maya Chen: Both, but we prefer API. Console for humans.

[12:30] Evan Brooks: Also we need to know how to pick the numbers. Like “max 16” is arbitrary until we understand tokens per second.

[12:38] Vanessa Ortiz: Yep. Part of the rollout is better dashboards: throughput, saturation, queue depth, desired vs bounded capacity. Then you can run experiments.

[12:50] Roberto Alvarez: Today we see some of that, but it’s not clear when a bound is the reason.

[12:54] Lauren Bishop: Right. Today it’s “autoscaled to N,” but not “autoscaler wanted N+4 and was clamped.” That’s exactly what we’re adding.

[13:06] Anika Patel: For me, I want a report like “hours at max bound” and “what would spend have been without the bound.” Is that possible?

[13:15] Lauren Bishop: We can get close. We can show you requested desired vs bounded desired, which is basically what would have happened. Translating that into spend is feasible but might be later than v1.

[13:28] Liam O'Rourke: We can also do an analysis with you based on metrics.

[13:32] Maya Chen: OK. Timeline wise, when do we get this?

[13:36] Lauren Bishop: We’re targeting a pilot in a couple regions first, behind a feature flag. I don’t want to promise an exact date on this call, but think weeks, not quarters, for pilot. GA would be after we validate safety and on-call readiness.

[13:55] Roberto Alvarez: So pilot like June-ish?

[13:58] Lauren Bishop: That’s directionally right.

[14:02] Vanessa Ortiz: The reason for the staged rollout is we need to validate anti-oscillation, cooldowns, and edge cases like “min > max” and region shortages.

[14:12] Evan Brooks: Min > max should be rejected, right.

[14:15] Vanessa Ortiz: Yes. Validation at the control plane.

[14:18] Maya Chen: What about per-time-of-day bounds? Like max higher during business hours.

[14:24] Lauren Bishop: Not in v1. We’ve heard it, but it complicates semantics and compliance. V1 is per-deployment static min/max with optional predictive mode. But you can change it via API with audit logs, with rate limits.

[14:42] Anika Patel: I’m okay with that. As long as we can do an approved change for special events.

[14:49] Liam O'Rourke: What about “burst capacity”? Like allow going above max for a short time.

[14:55] Maya Chen: No. That defeats the cap.

[14:58] Roberto Alvarez: Yeah, and it becomes a slippery thing.

[15:02] Vanessa Ortiz: Cool. Then hard max is straightforward.

[15:06] Liam O'Rourke: Let’s dig into the unpredictable bursts. Evan, you said incident response. Are those correlated with any internal signal you have? Like you open an incident, or a status page event.

[15:18] Evan Brooks: We have PagerDuty incidents. But that’s not necessarily aligned with user traffic.

[15:24] Roberto Alvarez: And I don’t want the autoscaler to depend on PagerDuty.

[15:27] Vanessa Ortiz: Yeah, we probably shouldn’t. For bursts, reactive needs to be fast. That means two things: keep enough baseline (min), and have scale-up behavior that’s not too conservative. Predictive helps for the known ramps. It won’t help for true surprises.

[15:47] Maya Chen: Understood.

[15:50] Lauren Bishop: Another piece: cooldowns and anti-oscillation. We’re adding dampening so the autoscaler doesn’t thrash up/down when signals are noisy.

[16:01] Roberto Alvarez: Thrash is one of our concerns. We’ve seen it with other systems.

[16:05] Evan Brooks: We also do continuous batching. Sometimes throughput increases without adding replicas, and queue depth changes. So signals can be weird.

[16:15] Vanessa Ortiz: Yes, batching can change the relationship between queue depth and utilization. That’s why we look at multiple signals and have safety rails.

[16:25] Liam O'Rourke: Quick check—are you primarily doing chat generation or also embeddings/rerank.

[16:31] Evan Brooks: Mostly chat generation. Long-ish contexts. Some tool calling. I heard you say “function calling” in docs.

[16:39] Liam O'Rourke: Yep.

[16:41] Maya Chen: Another requirement: We need deterministic behavior. Like if we set max, it must always enforce it. And we need to prove it during an audit.

[16:52] Lauren Bishop: Yep. That’s exactly why we’re treating bounds as hard invariants, and we’re logging decisions. We want “policy evaluation is deterministic,” which means the autoscaler loop records inputs and outputs and the clamp.

[17:08] Roberto Alvarez: Is that going to explode log volume?

[17:11] Vanessa Ortiz: It’s a concern. We’ll do it as structured events with sampling thresholds and keep cardinality under control. We don’t want per-request logs. It’s per scaling decision and per config change.

[17:24] Anika Patel: And retention? We might need 90 days.

[17:27] Lauren Bishop: For enterprise, we can support longer retention, and export to your SIEM if needed. We should align on your requirement.

[17:36] Maya Chen: 90 days is fine for most. For some, 1 year. But that’s probably a later discussion.

[17:42] Liam O'Rourke: We can loop in security folks if needed.

[17:46] Evan Brooks: Can we talk about “predictive” for a second. Like how confident do you have to be to scale ahead? I don’t want it scaling up every day based on old data.

[17:57] Vanessa Ortiz: Totally. The plan is to incorporate confidence and error tracking. If the predictor is consistently wrong, we can dial it back or disable it. And you can set predictive mode to “enabled but fallback to reactive” automatically if predictions are stale.

[18:16] Roberto Alvarez: But reactive always runs.

[18:18] Vanessa Ortiz: Yes. Reactive is always part of the arbitration.

[18:22] Lauren Bishop: Think of it as a multi-signal decision: prediction suggests a target, reactive suggests a target, then we pick a desired, then clamp to bounds, then apply cooldowns.

[18:34] Maya Chen: That’s helpful.

[18:36] Liam O'Rourke: Let’s get specific. If you had this feature today, what would you set?

[18:42] Maya Chen: Min 8, max 16. Probably.

[18:45] Anika Patel: Yeah, that matches our budget model.

[18:48] Roberto Alvarez: But I might push min to 10 if we keep getting morning pain.

[18:54] Evan Brooks: The min is also about cold start. If we keep 10, it’s smoother.

[18:58] Vanessa Ortiz: That’s exactly the kind of tuning we want to support. And the dashboard will show you the impact—how often you’re queueing at min, etc.

[19:10] Liam O'Rourke: Are you okay with a pilot where we enable bounds first, and predictive later? Or do you need both at once.

[19:18] Maya Chen: Bounds first would already be huge.

[19:21] Roberto Alvarez: Yeah, max cap first.

[19:23] Anika Patel: Please. (laughs)

[19:26] Lauren Bishop: Great. That’s also our phased rollout approach.

[19:30] Liam O'Rourke: On your side, what do you need to do to be ready? Any internal approvals?

[19:36] Maya Chen: We need to review it with our security and change control. But if it’s behind a feature flag and doesn’t change behavior unless we set bounds, we’re fine.

[19:47] Lauren Bishop: That’s a key design constraint: backward compatibility. Existing customers keep current behavior until enabled.

[19:56] Evan Brooks: If we set max and it clamps, does it change anything else? Like scale-down behavior.

[20:02] Vanessa Ortiz: Scale-down still happens, but not below min. And we add cooldowns to prevent oscillation.

[20:10] Roberto Alvarez: Cooldown defaults? Can we configure.

[20:12] Lauren Bishop: Yes, within reason. There will be validation boundaries so you can’t set like 0 seconds and thrash.

[20:22] Maya Chen: Another question: is max in replicas or GPUs. Because we think in dollars.

[20:28] Lauren Bishop: Internally we can express it in replicas, which maps to GPU units for your deployment. We’re also exploring expressing in “GPU quota.” For v1 it will likely show as replicas with an explanation of what that maps to.

[20:44] Anika Patel: As long as you tell me what it means.

[20:47] Liam O'Rourke: We can include a cost estimate in Console as a guide. It won’t be perfect but it helps.

[20:55] Evan Brooks: That’d be good.

[20:58] Roberto Alvarez: On the max hit state: can you emit a metric we can alert on in our system? We use Datadog.

[21:06] Vanessa Ortiz: Yes. We’ll have metrics like “desired replicas” vs “bounded desired replicas” and a counter for “hit max bound.” And queue depth and saturation.

[21:18] Roberto Alvarez: Great.

[21:20] Maya Chen: Another competitor question. Together said they can do reserved and burst. But they couldn’t give a hard cap; it was like “we’ll try.” We need hard.

[21:29] Lauren Bishop: Yeah, we’re aligning on “hard means hard.” The exception is the physical capacity shortage case for min, which is about availability, not policy.

[21:42] Liam O'Rourke: OK. We’ve got about 10–15 minutes left. I want to make sure we capture next steps and what data we need to set this up.

[21:52] Vanessa Ortiz: For predictive later, we’d want at least a couple weeks of history. For bounds, we mostly need to know your desired min/max and confirm the deployment IDs.

[22:04] Evan Brooks: We can send metrics. We don’t want to send raw logs.

[22:08] Liam O'Rourke: Metrics are fine. Even a screenshot can get us started.

[22:12] Anika Patel: I can share the budget model too. Like the spend cap and how it maps to GPU-hours.

[22:18] Lauren Bishop: That would be super helpful.

[22:21] Roberto Alvarez: One more: If we set max and we hit it, will Redwood page itself? Like do you get alerted.

[22:28] Vanessa Ortiz: We will have internal alerting as well, especially during pilot. But generally, hitting max isn’t always an incident—it might be an expected state. The difference is “max bound + sustained queue buildup,” which is customer-impacting.

[22:46] Roberto Alvarez: Right. So page on that, not just max.

[22:49] Vanessa Ortiz: Exactly.

[22:52] Maya Chen: Good.

[22:54] Liam O'Rourke: Lauren, can you share the rough rollout plan without overcommitting?

[22:59] Lauren Bishop: Yeah. We’re finalizing semantics and control plane schema. Then a pilot behind a feature flag for a small set of Dedicated customers in one region first. We’ll do canary + SRE readiness review. Then expand region-by-region. GA after we hit reliability and operability criteria: dashboards, alerts, runbook, audit logging.

[23:26] Maya Chen: Perfect.

[23:28] Evan Brooks: Is the pilot per-account or per-deployment.

[23:32] Lauren Bishop: Per-account and per-deployment. We can enable it narrowly.

[23:38] Evan Brooks: Great.

[23:40] Liam O'Rourke: Okay. Let’s capture action items. I’ll send recap. Maya, can you send your preferred bounds and any constraints. Roberto, send examples of the queue depth incidents.

[23:55] Maya Chen: Yep.

[23:56] Roberto Alvarez: Yep.

[23:58] Anika Patel: I’ll send the cap numbers.

[24:01] Evan Brooks: And I’ll pull the traffic ramps. Probably aggregated.

[24:06] Liam O'Rourke: Great. We should schedule a technical deep dive with Vanessa and Roberto/Evan to go through signals and dashboards.

[24:14] Vanessa Ortiz: Yep, happy to.

[24:16] Maya Chen: Next week works.

[24:18] Liam O'Rourke: Cool. We’ll follow up with times.

[24:22] Lauren Bishop: And I’ll share a short write-up on the semantics we discussed: requested desired, bounded desired, reasons, and what max-hit looks like.

[24:32] Maya Chen: Awesome.

[24:34] Liam O'Rourke: Anything else before we wrap?

[24:37] Roberto Alvarez: No, this was good.

[24:39] Anika Patel: Thanks.

[24:40] Evan Brooks: Thanks.

[24:41] Liam O'Rourke: Thanks everyone. Talk soon.

---
End of transcript.
